sound.text: Read the three song titles in order, Why, Me and ? (Cry), and they ask the question the EP is named for. It's the start of a breakup, and Jett2Fly gave each part its own sound. Why is slow and stripped down, with a simple beat that keeps the focus on SyWavy. Me pushes back, harder and heavier, with a few samples mixed in. ? (Cry) smooths it out into steady R&B and rap, built on the melody of Future's Solo.

inspirations.text: Samples the melody of Solo by Future

notes.title: Cry Me a River
notes.body: Justin Timberlake's 2002 song about a girlfriend who cheated. He won't be the one crying.

ref.name: Cry Me a River (Justin Timberlake song)

notes.title: Mac Miller
notes.body: The Pittsburgh artist behind Swimming and Circles. He splits the name across the line with a Miller beer on one end, and Mac also sounds like mack, slang for a smooth talker with women.

The breakup at the center of Why Me? and Hurts to Heal starts here. She'd met his family and he thought she was the one, and she insists she did nothing wrong. The title question grows out of that refusal.
The studio is home, and recording is how he works through it, with friends around and his phone in his hand. Making music to sort out his feelings becomes a thread through everything he makes.

notes.title: VLONE
notes.body: The streetwear label from the A$AP Mob circle, known for its big orange V. Its name comes from the motto live alone, die alone, so it's what he's wearing now that he's by himself.
By the end, the anger has burned off. She's blocked him and moved on, and he lets her go without hating anyone, the calmer side that Hurts to Heal picks up.

notes.title: Martin
notes.body: Martin Lawrence's 90s sitcom, where Martin and Gina were the couple everyone wanted to be and Pam was Gina's best friend. She wants to be Gina but doesn't have a Pam.

notes.title: Dunkin'
notes.body: The donut and coffee chain. Dunkin' sets up a slam dunk, and slam is also slang for the men she sleeps with.

notes.title: Usher
notes.body: The R&B star, whose 2016 single with Young Thug gives the line its opening words. His name also stands for the person who shows you to your seat.

notes.title: 50 Cent
notes.body: The Queens rapper and businessman. The joke is on sense and cents: his troubles don't add up, and the name is a sum of money.

notes.title: Bantu knots
notes.body: A protective hairstyle of small coiled knots, named for the Bantu-speaking peoples of Africa. Knot also sounds like not, so they're tied together and not together in the same breath.
He can't figure her out, loves her anyway, and ends the same thought cursing her. Three feelings in three lines, none of them canceling the others.

notes.title: Giveon
notes.body: The deep-voiced Long Beach R&B singer who broke through in 2020. One of his songs from that year shares its title with what he says he isn't.
The title for what they had is in the past tense now. The next line turns tense into the other kind, wound up and stressed.

notes.title: Amazon Alexa
notes.body: Amazon's voice assistant, there every time you call its name. That's how dependable he wanted her to be.
His mother tells him the pain is temporary. The song turns forward from there, to new stories and then a new girl calling.

notes.title: Slick Rick
notes.body: The London-born storyteller of 80s hip-hop, famous for his eye patch and gold chains. His breakout 1985 record with Doug E. Fresh is named for a live performance, which he admits he hasn't done yet.

notes.title: Lil Uzi Vert
notes.body: The Philadelphia artist's 2017 album Luv Is Rage 2 includes The Way Life Goes, one of its biggest songs. Rage and that title both fit in one line.
Scotti is a weed strain. It comes back on Wavy Life, in Fantasia.

notes.title: Nicki Minaj
notes.body: The Trinidad-born, Queens-raised rap star. Her last name sounds like ménage, as in a threesome.

notes.title: Star Crunch
notes.body: Little Debbie's chocolate-covered snack cake of crispy rice and caramel.
Being too nice got him burned, so he talks himself into the opposite. Then he admits that isn't who he is, says the lesson stuck and he's past it, and owns how it all sounds.
Being grounded means staying humble, and a basement sits under the ground, so the weed keeps him low both ways. The box is the vocal booth, filled with smoke.
The song ends with him saying he put everything he had into the track, then calling it done. The question mark in the title stays open.
